title: Russia Won't Invade NATO, but It Is Testing Whether NATO Holds Together
dek: Russia has no capacity for a ground offensive; its real goal is to corrode NATO's political cohesion — using drones, parcel bombs and grey zones to force the US to expose its divisions in a crisis.
why: The first half, on Russian hybrid warfare and NATO cohesion, is dense with analysis; the Middle East section in the second half is comparatively diffuse, but the detail about the Houthis using Claude to improve their missiles is worth hearing.
who: Readers following European security, NATO cohesion and the Middle East; engineers and investors interested in hybrid warfare, military AI applications and the shape of modern war.
skip: The podcast subscription promo segment (around 22:00) can be skipped.

points.h: No ground-invasion risk, but hybrid escalation is rising
points.body: Joshi says it plainly: there is no risk of a Russian conventional ground offensive against NATO, this is not the kind of alarm it was in January 2022. The entire security apparatus of Estonia and Finland exists to spot that kind of movement, and every port, naval base and forest route in western Russia is blanketed with intelligence and technical sensors. But another risk is rising: Russia's tolerance for hybrid operations below the Article V threshold is increasing. They have already used drones against Ukrainian cargo planes that may have been bound for Ukraine, put explosives in DHL parcels in Leipzig, and sabotaged power plants and railways across Europe. The question is: would they actually fire missiles at Polish facilities? Joshi thinks Russia is still quite cautious and wants to avoid dragging NATO into a broader conflict, but that debate is not settled in Europe.

points.h: Poland sounds the alarm loudest; the Baltics say things are fine
points.body: The most alarming signal this week came from Poland. Tusk said intelligence indicated Russia might attack Poland and other NATO allies — not a conventional ground attack, but drones and missiles landing on NATO territory that Russia could portray as accidents. But Latvia's leadership, including the defence minister and the president, said there is no reason to panic and no elevated operational risk. Estonia also said it sees no risk of Russia aggressing in that way. Joshi says he has spoken to intelligence officials in multiple countries and sees no reason to worry about a ground offensive. The disagreement is itself the signal: Poland is raising the alarm, the Baltic states are cooling things down, and Russia is watching who believes whom.

points.h: Russia's real goal is to corrode NATO cohesion
points.body: Joshi lays out Russia's political objective: not to conquer NATO territory or occupy Western Europe, but to weaken and break apart NATO's unity. The mechanism works like this: if a drone lands on Polish territory and blows up a warehouse, Russia says it was an accident, and then Trump says ‘I talked to Putin and he assured me it was an accident’ — and that lays the alliance's internal divisions bare. Under the Biden administration, Jake Sullivan would call the Russians and say that if this continues you are risking us joining the war on Ukraine's side, and we will retaliate. But under a Trump administration, does Russia really believe Trump would step into a crisis the same way? So Russia has an opportunity not only to push back against attacks on Russia, but to test NATO's cohesion and its boundaries.

points.h: On Ukraine, Trump criticises in public and supplies intelligence in private
points.body: Joshi says Trump's support for Ukraine is quite limited, far below the Biden era. The US has effectively let weapons aid lapse; Ukraine desperately needs Patriot interceptor missiles, but because the US has burned through so much in the Iran war, it has given Ukraine almost no interceptors recently. Diplomatically, the administration leans toward Russia and expects Ukraine to make concessions. But there are two exceptions: first, the new Graham bill, which the president has agreed to, would impose new sanctions on Russian entities and force Trump to levy tariffs on countries that buy Russian oil and do not reduce their purchases — in practice China and India, and possibly Central European countries. Second, Trump is quietly, not publicly, providing intelligence to Ukraine to help it strike Russian energy facilities. That is the strange reversal: Trump criticises Ukraine overall, yet secret assistance is still happening.

points.h: The Strait of Hormuz is still half-closed
points.body: The Trump administration insists this is not a war; Trump calls it an ‘excursion’. But the Strait of Hormuz remains largely closed, and oil traffic is far below pre-war levels. There is no deal with Iran, no resolution. Iran's nuclear programme has no formal limits, and there is no formal commitment to reopen Hormuz. Trump faces the midterms in a month and desperately needs to avoid a sharp escalation of the war that would send oil prices soaring. But politically he cannot make the concessions to Iran that a deal would require, because that would be too humiliating, too obviously equivalent to defeat, and would look catastrophic before an election. So it is a stalemate: Iran has considerable control over the strait, with occasional clashes — the US bombs Iranian coastal missile bases, Iran strikes tankers trying to pass through Hormuz.

points.h: The Houthis used Claude to improve their ballistic missiles
points.body: Joshi tells a striking detail: when Anthropic published its report on harmful uses of Claude, one of the examples was the Houthis using Claude to improve their ballistic missile programme. A group widely seen as technologically primitive is using the most advanced AI on Earth to improve the guidance systems of the ballistic missiles they fire at shipping in the Middle East. Mounk adds that being able — at least until being cut off — to access the most advanced American technology to strike America and America's allies is itself a fascinating story. This connects the Ukraine and Russia discussion to the Houthi discussion: in modern war, defensive capability dominates on the ground, but offensive capability dominates in the air.

points.h: Perception is the primary problem on the battlefield
points.body: Joshi offers a unifying framework for why ground defence dominates while air strikes still work: it is all about perception. To hit something, you first need to perceive it — find it on the battlefield, then fire at it. That is much harder than it sounds. Perception is the primary problem on the battlefield; actually firing is secondary. On the Ukrainian front line, this is a sensor-saturated environment: small drones everywhere, thermal cameras detecting movement at night, radar seeing through foliage, satellites targeting the area. Anything that moves gets hit — it is a kill zone. But you cannot perceive everywhere equally easily. Drones can see ten kilometres behind the battlefield, but fifty kilometres back, satellite coverage is patchy. It is like the fog of war in a real-time strategy game — you send units out and the fog lifts, but where you have not been remains fog. That is why Iran can still launch ballistic missiles, and why the Houthis can fire from the mountains of Yemen into the Red Sea.
